p.x:
Last weekend, my family went to the countryside. We stayed in a small house near a lake. Behind the house, there was a pond with lots of fish and a little stream.
In the morning, we took a ferry across the big river. Then my brother and I went in a canoe. The water was brown and muddy because it rained a lot last week. My dad said, "In the rainy months, the river rises. In summer, it's almost dry!"
In the afternoon, we went fishing, but we didn't catch anything. It was a lovely, relaxing day.

Bangkok was once called the "Venice of the East" because it had hundreds of canals. People travelled by boat, and markets were held on the water. Today, many canals have been filled in to make roads, but water is still an important part of life in the city.
The Chao Phraya River flows through the centre of Bangkok to the sea. Thousands of people use it every day. They wait at the pier for a river boat or take a water taxi to avoid the traffic jams. Along the riverside, there are temples, hotels and restaurants. Outside the city, visitors enjoy floating markets, where vendors paddle small boats full of fruit and food.
However, living near water has risks. During the rainy season, the water level can rise quickly. Heavy rain upstream sends huge amounts of water downstream towards Bangkok. When the city's drainage and sewers cannot cope, streets flood. A flash flood can happen in minutes. People protect their homes with sandbags, and the city uses giant pumps to remove the water. In some areas, people have even used a raft to move around.
On the coast, mangroves help protect the land from the sea. Tourists can kayak through them and see birds, crabs and fish. In the river delta, the rich soil is perfect for growing rice. Children often play on the riverbank in the evening.

In 2011, Thailand experienced its worst flooding in half a century. Months of heavy monsoon rain swelled the Chao Phraya and its tributaries, and as reservoirs in the north filled up, officials were forced to open the floodgates. The water spread slowly across the central floodplain, inundating farmland, homes and industrial estates. In some provinces, entire communities were submerged for weeks, and hundreds of people lost their lives. It took months for the water to subside.
The disaster revealed how vulnerable Bangkok is. The city lies only one or two metres above sea level, and parts of it are sinking as groundwater is pumped out. Meanwhile, rising sea levels caused by climate change threaten to push salt water further into the estuary. Some scientists warn that large areas of the capital could be underwater by the end of the century.
Governments have traditionally responded by building flood defences such as concrete embankments and walls. These can protect specific areas, but they may also push water onto neighbouring communities and prevent rivers from depositing the sediment that keeps land fertile. A growing number of planners now argue for working with nature rather than against it: restoring wetlands and mangroves, creating parks that can safely hold water, and designing buildings that can cope with occasional flooding. As one engineer put it, "We cannot stop the water. We can only decide where it goes."
